modules.title: History of Breast Cancer
modules.description: From the first written description of a breast tumour to digital mammography and AI-assisted imaging: how diagnosis and treatment changed over thousands of years.

sections.title: Why the history matters
sections.body:
Breast cancer has been described for thousands of years. For most of that time, doctors could recognise a hard lump in the breast but had no way to cure it.

Over the last two centuries, understanding of how cancer grows and spreads changed treatment from very large operations towards smaller, more precise surgery, combined with medicines that target how a particular cancer behaves. Screening with mammography made it possible to find many cancers before they can be felt.
sections.advanced: The dates below are the ones given by major cancer organisations. Where an exact year is not well established, a period is given instead.

items.label: About 3000 BCE (ancient Egypt)
items.title: The first written description
items.text: The Edwin Smith Papyrus, an ancient Egyptian medical text, describes bulging tumours of the breast. It states that there is no treatment.
items.note: It is the oldest known written description of what is believed to be breast cancer, and shows the disease is not new.

items.label: About 400 BCE (ancient Greece)
items.title: The word 'cancer'
items.text: The Greek physician Hippocrates is credited with first using the word for cancer, comparing a tumour to a crab ('karkinos' in Greek).
items.note: The names we still use today come from this period, even though the ideas about what caused cancer were later shown to be wrong.

items.title: Early clues about hormones
items.text: The Italian physician Bernardino Ramazzini noticed that nuns rarely had cervical cancer but had high rates of breast cancer, and wondered whether not having children played a role.
items.note: It was an early observation linking breast cancer to reproductive and hormonal factors, which later research confirmed.

items.label: Late 1800s
items.title: Radical mastectomy
items.text: Surgeons developed the radical mastectomy, a large operation removing the breast, the chest muscles underneath and the lymph nodes under the arm.
items.note: It was based on the idea that cancer spreads outward step by step, and it became the standard operation for most of the 20th century.

items.title: Hormones and breast cancer
items.text: Removing the ovaries was shown to slow breast cancer.
items.note: This suggested that some breast cancers depend on hormones made by the ovaries (later identified as estrogen) and led, decades later, to hormone therapy.

items.label: 1960s
items.title: Mammography
items.text: The mammogram, a low-dose X-ray of the breast, was developed as a practical test.
items.note: It made it possible to find breast cancer before it can be felt, and it remains the main screening test.

items.title: Tamoxifen
items.text: The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved tamoxifen, a drug that blocks hormone activity without the need for surgery.
items.note: It became one of the most widely used hormone therapies for hormone receptor-positive breast cancer.

items.label: Late 1900s
items.title: Breast-conserving surgery
items.text: About a century after the radical mastectomy, studies showed that removing only the tumour with a margin of normal tissue (lumpectomy) worked as well for many early breast cancers.
items.note: Many patients could keep their breast, and surgery became less extensive.

items.label: 1990s
items.title: BRCA genes
items.text: The BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes were identified. Harmful inherited changes in them greatly increase the risk of breast and ovarian cancer.
items.note: Genetic testing became possible for families at high risk.

items.title: Targeted therapy for HER2
items.text: The FDA approved trastuzumab, a drug that blocks the HER2 protein, which drives the growth of some breast cancers.
items.note: It was a landmark targeted therapy and changed the outlook for HER2-positive breast cancer.

items.label: Today
items.title: Precision medicine and AI-assisted imaging
items.text: Treatment is guided by tumour biology (ER, PR, HER2 and other biomarker tests), with targeted drugs and, for some triple-negative cancers, immunotherapy. Digital mammography and 3D mammography (tomosynthesis) are widely used. Artificial intelligence tools are being developed and tested to help radiologists read mammograms.
items.note: AI is a support tool: a radiologist and the full diagnostic process are still needed. The AI on this website is for research and education only.

modules.title: Understanding Breast Cancer
modules.description: What breast cancer is, how the breast is built, how normal cells become cancer cells, and the difference between benign and malignant conditions.

sections.title: What is breast cancer?
sections.body:
Breast cancer is a disease in which cells in the breast grow out of control. Most breast cancers start in the ducts (the tubes that carry milk to the nipple) or the lobules (the glands that make milk).

Breast cancer mostly affects women, but men can get it too, because men also have a small amount of breast tissue.

sections.title: Basic breast anatomy
sections.body:
The breast is made of:
- Lobules: small glands that can make milk.
- Ducts: thin tubes that carry milk from the lobules to the nipple.
- Fatty and connective tissue: surrounds and supports the lobules and ducts and gives the breast its shape.
- Blood vessels and lymph vessels: lymph vessels carry fluid to lymph nodes, many of which are in the armpit (axillary lymph nodes).

The breast lies on the chest muscle (pectoralis) over the ribs.

sections.title: How normal cells work
sections.body:
The body is made of cells. Normal cells grow and divide to make new cells when the body needs them. When cells become old or damaged, they die and are replaced.

This process is tightly controlled by the cell's genes, which act like instructions telling the cell when to grow, divide, repair itself or die.

sections.title: How cancer develops
sections.body:
Cancer starts when changes in genes (mutations) disrupt this control. A cell may keep dividing when it should stop, or fail to die when it should. Over time, these cells can build up and form a lump called a tumour.

Most gene changes that lead to breast cancer happen during a person's lifetime. A smaller number are inherited from a parent, such as harmful changes in the BRCA1 or BRCA2 genes.
sections.advanced: Cancer usually develops through several changes over time rather than a single event. Some cells first look abnormal (atypical) without being cancer. Cancer cells that stay inside the duct or lobule where they started are called 'in situ'. When they break through the wall of the duct or lobule into the surrounding tissue, the cancer is called 'invasive'.

sections.title: Normal cells compared with cancer cells

items.title: Growth
items.text: Normal cells grow only when needed. Cancer cells keep growing and dividing.
items.label: Control

items.title: Appearance
items.text: Normal cells look regular and organised under the microscope. Cancer cells often look irregular, and the more abnormal they look, the higher the tumour grade.
items.label: Microscope

items.title: Staying in place
items.text: Normal cells stay where they belong. Cancer cells can invade nearby tissue.
items.label: Invasion

items.title: Repair and death
items.text: Damaged normal cells are repaired or die. Cancer cells can ignore these signals.
items.label: Lifespan

sections.title: How cancer may spread
sections.body:
Invasive breast cancer can spread through lymph vessels to lymph nodes, most often those under the arm, and through the blood to other parts of the body.

When breast cancer spreads to distant organs, such as the bones, liver, lungs or brain, it is called metastatic or stage IV breast cancer. It is still breast cancer, not bone or lung cancer, because the cells came from the breast.

sections.title: Benign and malignant breast conditions
sections.body:
Many breast lumps and changes are not cancer.
- Benign (non-cancerous) conditions do not spread to other parts of the body. Examples are cysts (fluid-filled sacs) and fibroadenomas (solid, smooth lumps).
- Malignant means cancer: cells that can invade nearby tissue and spread.

> Only tests such as imaging and, when needed, a biopsy can tell whether a breast change is benign or malignant. Any new or changing breast change should be checked by a doctor.

modules.title: Breast Cancer Classification
modules.description: The four ways doctors describe a breast cancer: where it started, its molecular subtype (ER, PR, HER2, Ki-67), its grade, and its stage.

sections.title: Four ways to describe one cancer
sections.body:
Doctors describe each breast cancer in several ways at once. Together these help predict how the cancer may behave and which treatments are likely to help.
- Origin: where in the breast it started and whether it is in situ or invasive.
- Molecular subtype: what receptors and proteins the cancer cells have.
- Histological grade: how abnormal the cells look under the microscope.
- Stage: how large the cancer is and how far it has spread.

sections.title: A. Classification by origin
sections.body: 'In situ' means the abnormal cells are still inside the duct or lobule where they started. 'Invasive' (or infiltrating) means the cells have grown through the wall into the surrounding breast tissue, from where they can spread.

items.label: In situ · non-invasive
items.title: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)
items.text: Abnormal cells line the milk ducts but have not spread into nearby breast tissue. It is called stage 0 breast cancer.
items.note: It is often found on a mammogram as tiny calcium deposits. It is usually treated because it can become invasive.

items.label: Invasive · most common
items.title: Invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC)
items.text: Cancer that starts in a duct and grows into the surrounding breast tissue. It is the most common type of invasive breast cancer.
items.note: Sometimes reported as invasive breast cancer 'of no special type'.

items.label: Not cancer · risk marker
items.title: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)
items.text: Abnormal cells in the lobules. Despite the name, LCIS is not considered cancer.
items.note: It is a sign of a higher chance of developing breast cancer in either breast, so closer follow-up may be advised.

items.label: Invasive
items.title: Invasive lobular carcinoma (ILC)
items.text: Cancer that starts in the lobules and grows into nearby tissue. It is the second most common invasive type.
items.note: It may grow in a line of single cells and can be harder to see on a mammogram than IDC.

items.label: Less common
items.title: Other types
items.text: Less common types include inflammatory breast cancer, Paget disease of the breast, and special types such as tubular, mucinous and medullary carcinoma. Phyllodes tumours and angiosarcoma are rare.
items.note: See 'Types of Breast Cancer' for details.

sections.title: B. Classification by molecular subtype
sections.body:
Breast cancer cells are tested for proteins that act as 'receptors' or growth signals. The results describe the cancer's biology and guide treatment.
- Estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR): if present, the cancer is 'hormone receptor-positive' and its growth may be fuelled by these hormones. Hormone therapy can then help.
- HER2: a protein that helps cells grow. Cancers with too much HER2 are 'HER2-positive' and can be treated with drugs that target HER2.
- Ki-67: a marker of how many cells are dividing. A higher Ki-67 suggests faster growth.

rows: Luminal A
ER and/or PR positive, HER2 negative, low Ki-67
Tends to grow more slowly; usually treated with hormone therapy
Luminal B
ER and/or PR positive, HER2 positive or negative, higher Ki-67
Tends to grow faster than luminal A; may need chemotherapy and/or HER2 drugs as well as hormone therapy
HER2-positive (HER2-enriched)
HER2 positive, ER and PR negative
Can grow faster, but HER2-targeted drugs are effective
Triple-negative
ER negative, PR negative, HER2 negative
Hormone therapy and HER2 drugs do not work; treated with chemotherapy and sometimes immunotherapy

sections.advanced: Molecular subtypes were first defined by studying the pattern of genes active in tumours. In everyday care, doctors usually estimate the subtype from ER, PR, HER2 and Ki-67 testing on the biopsy, and sometimes from multigene tests that help decide whether chemotherapy is likely to help. Labs report HER2 as 0, 1+, 2+ or 3+; '2+' results are checked with another test. Cancers with low HER2 levels ('HER2-low') may be eligible for some newer HER2-directed drugs.

sections.title: C. Classification by histological grade

items.label: Grade 1
items.title: Well differentiated (low grade)
items.text: Cells look more like normal breast cells and tend to grow slowly.

items.label: Grade 2
items.title: Moderately differentiated (intermediate grade)
items.text: Cells look somewhat abnormal and grow faster than grade 1.

items.label: Grade 3
items.title: Poorly differentiated (high grade)
items.text: Cells look very different from normal cells and tend to grow and spread faster.

sections.body:
The grade describes how abnormal the cancer cells look under a microscope and how quickly they seem to be dividing.

> Grade is not the same as stage. Grade describes what the cells look like; stage describes how big the cancer is and how far it has spread. A small, early-stage cancer can still be high grade.
sections.advanced: Pathologists commonly use the Nottingham grading system, which scores three features from 1 to 3: how much the cells form normal-looking gland structures (tubule formation), how varied the nuclei look (nuclear pleomorphism), and how many cells are dividing (mitotic count). The total score gives grade 1, 2 or 3.

sections.title: D. Classification by stage
sections.body:
Stage describes the size of the cancer and how far it has spread. It is based on the TNM system:
- T (tumour): the size of the main tumour and whether it has grown into the skin or chest wall.
- N (nodes): whether cancer has reached nearby lymph nodes, and how many.
- M (metastasis): whether cancer has spread to distant parts of the body.

Stages run from 0 (non-invasive) to IV (spread to distant organs). The 'Breast Cancer Stages' module explains each stage.

> Clinical stage is based on examination, imaging and biopsy before surgery. Pathological stage uses what is found in the tissue and lymph nodes removed during surgery. The two can differ.
sections.advanced: In current staging, the TNM findings are combined with tumour grade and biomarker status (ER, PR and HER2) to give a 'prognostic stage'. This is why two cancers of the same size and spread can be given different stages.

modules.title: Types of Breast Cancer
modules.description: Invasive ductal and lobular carcinoma, DCIS, inflammatory breast cancer, triple-negative and HER2-positive cancers, Paget disease and breast cancer in men.

sections.title: Why the type matters
sections.body: The type of breast cancer is identified from the biopsy. Together with the stage and the receptor results, it helps the care team plan treatment. The descriptions below are general; each person's cancer is different.

items.label: What it is
items.title: The most common invasive type
items.text: Cancer that starts in a milk duct and grows into the surrounding breast tissue.

items.label: Possible symptoms
items.title: Often a lump
items.text: May be found as a lump or on a screening mammogram before any symptoms.

items.label: Diagnosis
items.title: Imaging and biopsy
items.text: Mammogram and ultrasound, then a core needle biopsy with ER, PR and HER2 testing.

items.label: Treatment
items.title: Depends on stage and receptors
items.text: Surgery, often radiation, and depending on the cancer, hormone therapy, chemotherapy, HER2-targeted therapy or other medicines.

items.label: What it is
items.title: Starts in the lobules
items.text: Cancer that starts in the milk-producing lobules and spreads into nearby tissue.

items.label: Characteristics
items.title: Can be harder to see
items.text: Cells often grow in single lines, so it may feel like a thickening rather than a distinct lump and can be harder to see on a mammogram. It is usually hormone receptor-positive.

items.label: Diagnosis
items.title: Imaging and biopsy
items.text: Mammogram, ultrasound and sometimes MRI, followed by a biopsy.

items.label: Treatment
items.title: Similar approach to IDC
items.text: Surgery, radiation when indicated, and usually hormone therapy; other treatments depend on the cancer.

items.label: What it is
items.title: Stage 0, non-invasive
items.text: Abnormal cells inside the milk ducts that have not spread into surrounding tissue.

items.label: Symptoms
items.title: Usually none
items.text: Most DCIS is found on a screening mammogram, often as small calcium deposits (microcalcifications).

items.label: Diagnosis
items.title: Biopsy
items.text: A biopsy of the area seen on the mammogram confirms it.

items.label: Treatment
items.title: To prevent invasive cancer
items.text: Usually surgery (lumpectomy or mastectomy), often followed by radiation after lumpectomy; hormone therapy may be offered for hormone receptor-positive DCIS.

items.label: What it is
items.title: A rare, fast-growing type
items.text: Cancer cells block lymph vessels in the skin of the breast.

items.label: Symptoms
items.title: Usually no lump
items.text: The breast becomes red, swollen and may look bruised; the skin can look like orange peel. Symptoms often appear quickly, over weeks.

items.label: Diagnosis
items.title: Biopsy of breast and skin
items.text: Imaging and a biopsy. It can be mistaken for an infection, so symptoms that do not improve need checking.

items.label: Treatment
items.title: Combined treatment
items.text: Usually chemotherapy first, then surgery (mastectomy) and radiation, with targeted or hormone therapy depending on the cancer.

items.label: What it is
items.title: ER, PR and HER2 negative
items.text: The cancer cells lack estrogen and progesterone receptors and do not have extra HER2.

items.label: Characteristics
items.title: Often grows faster
items.text: It is more common in younger women and in people with a BRCA1 mutation.

items.label: Diagnosis
items.title: Receptor testing
items.text: Found through ER, PR and HER2 testing on the biopsy.

items.label: Treatment
items.title: Chemotherapy-based
items.text: Hormone therapy and HER2 drugs do not work. Chemotherapy is the main treatment; immunotherapy and other drugs may be used for some patients.

items.label: What it is
items.title: Too much HER2
items.text: The cancer cells make too much of the HER2 protein, which helps them grow.

items.label: Characteristics
items.title: Can grow faster
items.text: It can grow and spread faster than HER2-negative cancer, but it responds to HER2-targeted drugs.

items.label: Diagnosis
items.title: HER2 testing
items.text: Tested on the biopsy with immunohistochemistry (IHC) and, if unclear, in situ hybridisation (ISH).

items.label: Treatment
items.title: HER2-targeted therapy
items.text: HER2-targeted drugs such as trastuzumab are usually combined with chemotherapy, plus surgery and radiation as needed.

items.label: What it is
items.title: Affects the nipple and areola
items.text: A rare type in which cancer cells collect in or around the nipple. Most people with it also have DCIS or invasive cancer elsewhere in the same breast.

items.label: Symptoms
items.title: Nipple skin changes
items.text: Itching, tingling or redness; flaky, crusty or thickened skin; a flattened nipple; yellowish or bloody discharge. It can be mistaken for eczema.

items.label: Diagnosis
items.title: Skin biopsy
items.text: A biopsy of the nipple skin, plus breast imaging to look for other tumours.

items.label: Treatment
items.title: Surgery
items.text: Surgery to remove the nipple and areola with breast-conserving surgery or mastectomy, followed by other treatment depending on what is found.

items.label: What it is
items.title: Rare but real
items.text: Men have a small amount of breast tissue behind the nipple, and cancer can develop there. According to the WHO, about 0.5–1% of breast cancers occur in men.

items.label: Symptoms
items.title: Often a lump near the nipple
items.text: A painless lump, nipple changes or discharge. Men may delay seeking help because they do not expect breast cancer.

items.label: Risk factors
items.title: Including BRCA2
items.text: Older age, family history, BRCA2 mutations and high estrogen levels are among the risk factors.

items.label: Treatment
items.title: Similar to women
items.text: Usually mastectomy, with radiation, hormone therapy, chemotherapy or targeted therapy depending on the cancer. Most are hormone receptor-positive.

modules.title: Breast Cancer Stages
modules.description: Stage 0 to stage IV explained with the TNM system, and why clinical and pathological stage can differ.

sections.title: What staging tells you
sections.body: The stage describes how much cancer there is and where it is in the body. It helps the care team plan treatment and estimate the outlook. Staging uses the results of examination, imaging, biopsy and, after surgery, the tissue removed.

items.label: T
items.title: Primary tumour
items.text: How large the main tumour is and whether it has grown into the skin or chest wall. Tis means in situ; T1 to T4 go from small to larger or more extensive.

items.label: N
items.title: Regional lymph nodes
items.text: Whether cancer has reached nearby lymph nodes (under the arm, near the breastbone or collarbone) and how many. N0 means none.

items.label: M
items.title: Distant metastasis
items.text: Whether cancer has spread to distant parts of the body. M0 means no distant spread; M1 means it has spread.

items.label: Stage 0
items.title: Non-invasive
items.text: Abnormal cells have not spread beyond the duct where they started, such as DCIS.

items.label: Stage I
items.title: Early, small
items.text: A small invasive cancer confined to the breast, or with a very small amount of cancer in nearby lymph nodes (IA and IB).

items.label: Stage II
items.title: Early, larger or in nodes
items.text: Cancer in the breast, in a few nearby lymph nodes, or both (IIA and IIB).

items.label: Stage III
items.title: Locally advanced
items.text: Cancer has spread to more lymph nodes near the breast, or to the skin of the breast or the chest wall (IIIA, IIIB, IIIC). Inflammatory breast cancer is at least stage IIIB.

items.label: Stage IV
items.title: Metastatic
items.text: Cancer has spread to distant parts of the body, such as the bones, liver, lungs or brain.

sections.title: Clinical and pathological stage
sections.body:
- Clinical stage is given first, before any surgery, from the physical exam, imaging and biopsy.
- Pathological stage is given when surgery is the first treatment, using what is found in the breast tissue and lymph nodes removed.

> The two can differ: surgery sometimes finds more or less cancer than imaging suggested. If chemotherapy or other treatment is given before surgery, the stage after treatment is recorded separately.
sections.advanced: Current staging also combines TNM with tumour grade and ER, PR and HER2 status to give a 'prognostic stage'. Two cancers of the same size and spread can therefore have different stages. Stage is one of several factors used to plan treatment.

modules.title: Causes and Risk Factors
modules.description: Age, family history, BRCA genes, hormones, lifestyle and previous breast conditions: what raises risk, what is uncertain, and what a risk factor really means.

sections.title: What a risk factor means
sections.body:
A risk factor is anything that raises the chance of getting a disease.

> Having a risk factor, or even several, does not mean you will get breast cancer. Many people with risk factors never develop it, and many people with breast cancer have no risk factor other than being a woman and getting older.

sections.title: Established risk factors you cannot change

items.label: Sex
items.title: Being a woman
items.text: Breast cancer is much more common in women than in men.

items.label: Age
items.title: Getting older
items.text: Risk increases with age; most breast cancers are found in women over 50.

items.label: Genes
items.title: Inherited gene changes
items.text: Harmful inherited changes in genes such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 greatly increase risk, although some people with these changes never develop cancer.

items.label: Family
items.title: Family history
items.text: Having close relatives (such as a mother, sister or daughter) with breast or ovarian cancer increases risk.

items.label: History
items.title: Previous breast cancer or conditions
items.text: A previous breast cancer, and some benign conditions such as atypical hyperplasia or LCIS, increase risk.

items.label: Hormones
items.title: Reproductive history
items.text: Starting periods early or menopause late means longer exposure to hormones and slightly higher risk.

items.label: Density
items.title: Dense breasts
items.text: Dense breast tissue on a mammogram is linked to higher risk and can make cancers harder to see.

items.label: Radiation
items.title: Chest radiation at a young age
items.text: Radiation to the chest, for example for lymphoma in childhood or young adulthood, increases risk.

items.label: Alcohol
items.title: Drinking alcohol
items.text: Risk rises with the amount of alcohol drunk.

items.label: Weight
items.title: Overweight after menopause
items.text: Having more body fat after menopause increases risk.

items.label: Activity
items.title: Physical inactivity
items.text: Regular physical activity is linked to lower risk.

items.label: Hormones
items.title: Some hormone therapy after menopause
items.text: Combined estrogen-plus-progestin hormone therapy after menopause increases risk.

items.label: Pregnancy
items.title: Childbearing and breastfeeding
items.text: Not having children, or having a first child after 30, slightly increases risk; breastfeeding may slightly lower it.

sections.title: Factors with uncertain or no proven effect
sections.body:
Research has not shown a clear link, or results have been mixed, for factors such as:
- Diet and vitamins, such as fat intake, soy or vitamin D.
- Some chemicals in the environment.
- Night shift work.

Antiperspirants, bras, breast implants, and abortion or miscarriage are listed by the American Cancer Society as disproven or controversial risk factors.
sections.advanced: Cancer organisations update these lists as new studies are published; the American Cancer Society keeps a separate page on unclear, disproven and controversial risk factors (see references).

sections.title: When genetic counselling may help
sections.body: A doctor may suggest genetic counselling and testing if you have a strong family history of breast or ovarian cancer, a relative with a known BRCA mutation, a personal history of breast cancer at a young age, or breast cancer in a male relative. A genetic counsellor explains what testing can and cannot tell you before you decide.

modules.title: Signs and Symptoms
modules.description: The breast changes worth getting checked, how to check your own breasts (Touch, Look, Check), and when to see a doctor. Most lumps are not cancer, but new changes should be looked at.

sections.title: Know what is normal for you
sections.body:
Breasts change with age, periods, pregnancy and weight. Knowing how your breasts usually look and feel makes it easier to notice something new.

> Most breast lumps and changes are not cancer. But only a doctor, with tests if needed, can tell what a change is.

sections.title: Breast self-examination: Touch, Look, Check
sections.body:
Checking your own breasts helps you learn what is normal for you, so a new change is easier to notice. There is no special technique and you do not need any training. The most important thing is to check regularly.

> A self-check does not replace screening. Self-exams alone are not enough to find breast cancer early, so keep going to the mammograms recommended for you, and tell your doctor about any change, even if your last mammogram was normal.

items.title: Touch
items.text: Feel your whole breast area, including up to your collarbone and into your armpits.
items.note: Feel for a lump, thickening, or any area that feels different from the rest or from the other side.

items.title: Look
items.text: Look at your breasts and nipples for any change in size, shape or skin.
items.note: For example puckering or dimpling, redness or a rash, crusting around the nipple, a nipple that has turned inward, or fluid from a nipple.

items.title: Check
items.text: If you notice anything new or unusual for you, make an appointment with a doctor.
items.note: Most changes are not cancer, but getting a change checked is always better than waiting.

sections.advanced:
When and where: any time that suits you, for example in bed, in the shower or while getting dressed. Breasts can change during periods, pregnancy and menopause, so checking regularly helps you learn your own pattern.

Men can get breast cancer too, so men should also check their chest area and report any lump or nipple change.

items.label: Lump
items.title: A new lump or thickening
items.text: In the breast or armpit, often painless. A hard lump with irregular edges is more likely to be cancer, but cancers can also be soft or rounded.

items.label: Shape
items.title: Change in size or shape
items.text: One breast changes size or shape, or looks different from before.

items.label: Nipple
items.title: Nipple changes
items.text: A nipple that turns inward (when it did not before), changes position or shape, or has a rash or crusting.

items.label: Discharge
items.title: Nipple discharge
items.text: Fluid from the nipple that is not breast milk, especially if it is bloody or comes from one breast without squeezing.

items.label: Skin
items.title: Skin dimpling
items.text: Puckering or dimpling of the skin, sometimes looking like orange peel.

items.label: Colour
items.title: Redness or swelling
items.text: Redness, darkening, warmth or swelling of all or part of the breast.

items.label: Armpit
items.title: Changes around the armpit
items.text: A lump or swelling under the arm or around the collarbone.

items.label: Pain
items.title: Pain that does not go away
items.text: Breast pain alone is rarely a sign of cancer, but pain in one spot that does not go away should be checked.

sections.title: When to see a healthcare professional
sections.body:
See a doctor if you notice any new breast change, or a change that does not go away after your next period.
- Do not wait for a change to become painful.
- Get urgent care if the breast becomes red, hot and swollen with fever, or if symptoms change quickly over days or weeks.
- Keep going to screening appointments even if you have no symptoms, because many early cancers cause no symptoms at all.

modules.title: Diagnosis and Screening
modules.description: The diagnostic journey step by step, from a clinical breast exam and imaging to biopsy, pathology and biomarker tests, and how screening differs from diagnostic tests.

sections.title: Screening and diagnostic tests

rows: Who
People with no symptoms
People with a symptom or an abnormal screening result
Purpose
Find cancer early, before it can be felt
Find out what a specific change is
Typical test
Screening mammogram
Diagnostic mammogram, ultrasound, MRI, biopsy
Result
Normal, or called back for more tests
A diagnosis, or a plan for follow-up

sections.body: Being called back after a screening mammogram is common and usually does not mean cancer. It means more pictures or tests are needed.

items.title: Clinical breast examination
items.text: A doctor or nurse looks at and feels the breasts and armpits for lumps or other changes.
items.note: Tells the team where to look; it cannot show what a lump is.

items.title: Mammography
items.text: Low-dose X-ray images of the breast. A diagnostic mammogram takes extra views of the area of concern.
items.note: Shows masses, calcifications and distortions, and is reported with a BI-RADS category.

items.title: Breast ultrasound
items.text: Sound waves create images of the breast.
items.note: Shows whether a lump is a fluid-filled cyst or solid, and helps guide biopsies.

items.title: Breast MRI, when indicated
items.text: Magnets and radio waves, usually with contrast dye.
items.note: Used for some high-risk screening, to measure a known cancer, or when other tests are unclear. It is not needed for everyone.

items.title: Image-guided biopsy
items.text: A needle removes small samples of tissue, guided by ultrasound, mammography (stereotactic) or MRI.
items.note: A biopsy is the only way to confirm whether a change is cancer.

items.title: Histopathology
items.text: A pathologist examines the tissue under a microscope.
items.note: Confirms whether it is cancer, the type (for example IDC or ILC), whether it is in situ or invasive, and the grade.

items.title: Biomarker testing
items.text: The tissue is tested for ER, PR and HER2, and sometimes Ki-67 or multigene tests.
items.note: Shows the molecular subtype and which treatments are likely to help.

sections.title: After a diagnosis
sections.body: If cancer is found, further tests may be done to see whether it has spread, such as blood tests or scans of the chest, bones or abdomen, depending on the stage and symptoms. A multidisciplinary team of surgeons, oncologists, radiologists and pathologists then plans treatment together with the patient.

sections.title: About screening
sections.body: Screening recommendations, such as the age to start and how often to have mammograms, differ between countries and depend on personal risk. Talk with a doctor about what is right for you, especially if you have a family history or other risk factors.
sections.advanced: Screening has benefits (finding cancers earlier, when treatment may be simpler) and limits (false alarms that lead to extra tests, and finding some cancers that would never have caused harm). Organisations weigh these differently, which is why recommendations vary.

video.title: What You Should Know About Your Breast Diagnostic Appointment

modules.title: Mammography and BI-RADS
modules.description: How a mammogram works and an interactive guide to the BI-RADS categories 0 to 6 that radiologists use to report it.

sections.title: What a mammogram is
sections.body:
A mammogram is a low-dose X-ray of the breast. The breast is pressed between two plates for a few seconds to spread the tissue and get a clear picture. Usually two views of each breast are taken.
- 2D digital mammography takes flat images.
- Digital breast tomosynthesis (3D mammography) takes many images from different angles to build a layered picture, which can help in dense breasts.

Radiologists look for masses, tiny calcium deposits (microcalcifications), areas where the tissue looks distorted, and differences between the two breasts.
sections.advanced: The report also describes breast density: (a) almost entirely fatty, (b) scattered fibroglandular density, (c) heterogeneously dense, or (d) extremely dense. Dense tissue can hide cancers and is itself linked to slightly higher risk, so additional imaging is sometimes discussed.

sections.title: BI-RADS categories: interactive guide
sections.body: BI-RADS (Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System), developed by the American College of Radiology, is the standard way radiologists summarise a mammogram, ultrasound or breast MRI. Select a category to learn what it means.

items.title: Incomplete
items.text: The radiologist needs more imaging, or older mammograms to compare with, before giving a final assessment.
items.note: Usually more mammogram views (spot compression or magnification) and/or an ultrasound, or comparison with previous images.

items.title: Negative
items.text: Nothing abnormal to report. The breasts look symmetrical, with no masses, distortion or suspicious calcifications.
items.note: Continue routine screening as advised.

items.title: Benign
items.text: A definitely non-cancerous finding is present, such as benign calcifications, a simple cyst or a lymph node in the breast.
items.note: Continue routine screening as advised.

items.title: Probably benign
items.text: The finding is very likely benign; the chance of cancer is no more than 2%.
items.note: Repeat imaging in about 6 to 12 months, then regular checks until the area has been stable, usually for at least 2 years.

items.title: Suspicious
items.text: The finding does not definitely look like cancer, but cancer is possible. Often split into 4A (low), 4B (moderate) and 4C (high) suspicion.
items.note: A biopsy should be considered.

items.title: Highly suggestive of malignancy
items.text: The finding looks very much like cancer; the chance of cancer is at least 95%.
items.note: A biopsy is very strongly recommended.

items.title: Known biopsy-proven malignancy
items.text: Cancer has already been confirmed by biopsy. This category is used for imaging done before or during treatment.
items.note: Imaging helps plan treatment and see how well it is working.

sections.title: Why follow-up matters
sections.body:
A BI-RADS category is only useful if its recommendation is followed. Missing a recommended follow-up scan or biopsy can delay finding a cancer, while following it can often confirm that a finding is harmless.

> BI-RADS is an imaging assessment category, not a cancer stage. A BI-RADS 4 or 5 result does not mean cancer has been diagnosed; only a biopsy can confirm cancer. The AI result on this website is not a BI-RADS assessment.

video.title: Mayo Clinic Minute: What women need to know about mammograms

modules.title: Breast Cancer Treatment
modules.description: Local treatments (lumpectomy, mastectomy, radiation) and systemic treatments (chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy): what they are, when they may be used, and common side effects.

sections.title: How treatment is decided
sections.body:
Treatment is planned by a team of specialists together with the patient. It depends on:
- The type of breast cancer and its stage.
- Biomarkers: ER, PR and HER2 status, and sometimes other tests.
- The grade of the cancer.
- The person's age, general health and preferences.

> This information is general education. It does not recommend a treatment for any individual. Only your care team can advise what is right for you.

sections.title: Local treatment
sections.body: Local treatments treat the breast and nearby lymph nodes.

items.label: Surgery
items.title: Lumpectomy (breast-conserving surgery)
items.text: Removes the cancer with a margin of normal tissue, keeping most of the breast.
items.note: Usually followed by radiation. Side effects can include pain, swelling and a change in breast shape.

items.label: Surgery
items.title: Mastectomy
items.text: Removes the whole breast. It may be recommended for large or multiple tumours, or chosen by the patient.
items.note: Breast reconstruction can be done at the same time or later. Recovery usually takes a few weeks.

items.label: Radiation
items.title: Radiation therapy
items.text: High-energy rays kill cancer cells that may remain in the breast, chest wall or lymph node areas.
items.note: Commonly given after lumpectomy and sometimes after mastectomy. Side effects include tiredness and skin changes like sunburn in the treated area.

sections.title: Systemic treatment
sections.body: Systemic treatments are medicines that travel through the body. They may be given before surgery (neoadjuvant) to shrink a tumour, after surgery (adjuvant) to lower the chance of the cancer coming back, or for cancer that has spread.

items.label: Medicine
items.title: Chemotherapy
items.text: Drugs that kill fast-dividing cells, given in cycles, usually by drip or by mouth.
items.note: May be considered for higher-risk, HER2-positive or triple-negative cancers. Side effects can include tiredness, hair loss, nausea and a higher risk of infection; most improve after treatment ends.

items.label: Medicine
items.title: Hormone (endocrine) therapy
items.text: Blocks estrogen or lowers its levels, for example tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors.
items.note: Used for hormone receptor-positive cancers, often for 5 years or more. Side effects can include hot flushes, joint pain and, with some drugs, bone thinning.

items.label: Medicine
items.title: Targeted therapy
items.text: Drugs that act on specific features of cancer cells, such as HER2-targeted drugs (for example trastuzumab) or drugs for certain gene changes.
items.note: Used when the cancer has the target. Side effects depend on the drug; some HER2 drugs require heart monitoring.

items.label: Medicine
items.title: Immunotherapy
items.text: Helps the immune system recognise and attack cancer cells.
items.note: Used for some triple-negative breast cancers. It can cause inflammation in different organs, so it needs monitoring.

sections.title: Recovery and support
sections.body: Recovery depends on the treatments received. Common considerations include managing tiredness, looking after the skin during radiation, moving the arm and shoulder as advised after surgery, and attending follow-up appointments. Many hospitals offer specialist nurses, physiotherapy and emotional support. Clinical trials may also be an option to discuss with the care team.

modules.title: Surgery and Recovery
modules.description: Lumpectomy and mastectomy, sentinel and axillary lymph node surgery, breast reconstruction, recovering after surgery, lymphedema and follow-up.

items.label: Breast-conserving
items.title: Lumpectomy
items.text: Removes the tumour and a rim of normal tissue (the margin). If cancer cells are found at the edge, a second operation may be needed.
items.note: Usually followed by radiation therapy.

items.label: Whole breast
items.title: Mastectomy
items.text: Removes the breast. Types include simple (total) mastectomy and skin- or nipple-sparing mastectomy, which can help with reconstruction.
items.note: Some people choose to have both breasts removed; this is discussed with the surgeon.

items.label: Smaller operation
items.title: Sentinel lymph node biopsy
items.text: Finds and removes the first one to a few lymph nodes that the cancer would drain to, using a dye and/or a tracer.
items.note: If these are clear, other nodes usually do not need to be removed, which lowers the risk of side effects.

items.label: Larger operation
items.title: Axillary lymph node surgery (dissection)
items.text: Removes more lymph nodes from the armpit.
items.note: May be needed when cancer is found in several nodes. It has a higher risk of arm swelling (lymphedema).

sections.title: Breast reconstruction
sections.body:
Reconstruction rebuilds the shape of the breast after mastectomy. It can be done at the same time as the mastectomy or later.
- Implant-based reconstruction uses a silicone or saline implant.
- Tissue-flap (autologous) reconstruction uses tissue from another part of the body, such as the abdomen.
- Nipple reconstruction or tattooing can follow.

Some people choose not to have reconstruction and have a flat closure or use an external prosthesis. All of these are valid choices.

sections.title: Recovering after surgery
sections.body:
- Most people go home the same day or after a short stay.
- Drains may be left in for a few days to remove fluid.
- Pain usually improves over days to weeks; follow the team's advice on pain relief.
- Arm and shoulder exercises, as advised by the team or a physiotherapist, help restore movement.
- Contact the care team about fever, increasing redness, swelling or fluid at the wound.

sections.title: Lymphedema awareness
sections.body:
Lymphedema is long-lasting swelling caused by lymph fluid building up when lymph flow is disrupted, for example after lymph node surgery or radiation. It can develop months or years after treatment.
- Watch for swelling, heaviness or tightness in the arm, hand, breast or chest on the treated side.
- Report it early: treatment such as specialised massage, compression and exercise works best when started early.

sections.title: Follow-up appointments
sections.body: After treatment, regular follow-up visits check recovery, manage side effects and look for signs of the cancer returning. They usually include a physical exam and regular mammograms of the remaining breast tissue. Report any new symptoms between visits.

video.title: Ask Mayo Clinic Health System – Lumpectomy vs. Mastectomy

modules.title: Prevention and Survivorship
modules.description: Ways to lower risk, screening and genetic counselling discussions, follow-up care, emotional health and support during and after breast cancer.

sections.title: Lowering risk
sections.body:
There is no sure way to prevent breast cancer, and no lifestyle change can completely remove the risk. Some choices are linked to lower risk:
- Staying physically active.
- Keeping a healthy weight, especially after menopause.
- Limiting or avoiding alcohol.
- Breastfeeding, if possible.
- Discussing the risks and benefits of hormone therapy after menopause with a doctor.

These also benefit general health.
sections.advanced: For people at high risk, for example those with a BRCA mutation or a strong family history, doctors may discuss closer screening (sometimes including MRI), medicines that lower risk, or risk-reducing surgery. These decisions are personal and made with specialists.

sections.title: Screening and genetic counselling
sections.body: Talk with a doctor about when to start screening and how often, based on your age, country guidelines and personal risk. If you have a strong family history of breast or ovarian cancer, ask whether genetic counselling is right for you.

items.label: Follow-up
items.title: Follow-up care
items.text: Regular check-ups and mammograms, and continuing medicines such as hormone therapy as prescribed.

items.label: Body
items.title: Managing long-term effects
items.text: Tiredness, lymphedema, menopause symptoms, fertility questions and bone health can be addressed with the care team.

items.label: Mind
items.title: Emotional health
items.text: Fear of recurrence, anxiety and low mood are common. Counselling and support groups can help; ask your team for referrals.

items.label: People
items.title: Family support
items.text: Partners, children and friends may need information and support too. Being open about what helps can make a difference.

items.label: Resources
items.title: Support organisations
items.text: Organisations such as Breast Cancer Now, the American Cancer Society and the National Cancer Institute provide information and support services.

modules.title: Breast Augmentation and Implants
modules.description: What breast implants are, cosmetic augmentation and implants after mastectomy, possible complications, BIA-ALCL, and how to get mammograms when you have implants.

sections.title: What breast implants are
sections.body:
Breast implants are medical devices placed under the breast tissue or under the chest muscle. They are used to:
- increase breast size or change breast shape (augmentation),
- rebuild the breast after a mastectomy or an injury (reconstruction),
- replace earlier implants (revision surgery).

Two types are approved in the United States: saline-filled and silicone gel-filled. Both have a silicone outer shell. They come in different sizes, shapes, shell thicknesses and surface textures.

items.label: Fill
items.title: Saline implants
items.text: A silicone shell filled with sterile salt water.
items.note: If the shell leaks, the saline is absorbed by the body and the implant loses its size or shape (deflation).

items.label: Fill
items.title: Silicone gel implants
items.text: A silicone shell filled with silicone gel.
items.note: A leak often causes no symptoms (a "silent" rupture), so it may only be found with imaging.

items.label: Surface
items.title: Smooth or textured
items.text: The shell surface can be smooth or textured.
items.note: The risk of BIA-ALCL, a rare lymphoma, is higher with textured implants (see below).

sections.title: Breast augmentation: things to consider
sections.body:
Breast augmentation is surgery to make the breasts larger or change their shape with implants. Before deciding, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) asks people to know that:
- Breast implants are not lifetime devices. The longer you have them, the more likely complications become.
- You should expect to need more surgery (reoperation) at some point.
- Even when there are complications, removing or replacing implants may not be covered by insurance.
- In the US, the surgeon goes through a patient decision checklist with you, and you both sign it before surgery.

> Choose a qualified surgeon, ask about every risk, and take time to decide.

sections.title: Implants after a mastectomy
sections.body: Implants are one way to rebuild a breast after a mastectomy. Reconstruction can be done at the same time as the mastectomy (immediate) or months or even years later (delayed).

items.title: Tissue expander
items.text: Often a tissue expander is placed first under the skin or chest muscle and filled with saline or air over several visits.
items.note: This slowly makes room for the implant.

items.title: Implant
items.text: When the tissue has stretched and healed, usually 2 to 6 months later, the expander is replaced with a saline or silicone implant.
items.note: Sometimes the implant is placed during the mastectomy itself, without an expander.

items.title: Other choices
items.text: Reconstruction can also use your own tissue (a flap), a mix of both, or no reconstruction at all.
items.note: See "Surgery and Recovery" for these options.

sections.title: Possible complications
sections.body: The FDA lists these among the complications that can happen with breast implants. Smoking, obesity and diabetes can raise the chance of problems.

items.label: Common
items.title: Capsular contracture
items.text: Hard scar tissue forms around the implant and squeezes it.
items.note: Severe cases can cause pain or a changed shape and may need another operation.

items.label: Common
items.title: Rupture or deflation
items.text: The shell can tear or leak. Saline implants deflate; silicone ruptures are often silent.
items.note: MRI is the most effective way to find a silent rupture; ultrasound is an acceptable alternative if there are no symptoms.

items.label: Other
items.title: Other local problems
items.text: Breast pain, infection, fluid or blood collecting around the implant, uneven breasts, wrinkling, or the implant moving out of place.

items.label: Systemic
items.title: "Breast implant illness"
items.text: Some people report tiredness, memory problems, rash, "brain fog" or joint pain.
items.note: These symptoms are poorly understood. Some people report that they improved after the implants were removed.

sections.title: Implants and cancer
sections.body:
Breast implants have not been shown to increase the risk of breast cancer, or the chance of breast cancer coming back.

They have been linked to a rare cancer of the immune system called breast implant-associated anaplastic large cell lymphoma (BIA-ALCL). It is not breast cancer; it is a type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
- The risk is low, and higher with textured implants than with smooth ones. The filling (saline or silicone) does not appear to matter.
- The main signs are swelling that does not go away, a lump, or pain around the implant, often years after surgery.
- Treatment is removal of the implant and the scar capsule around it; some people also need chemotherapy or radiation.

> Swelling, a lump or pain around an implant, even years later, should be checked by a doctor.
sections.advanced: The FDA has also received reports of other rare cancers, such as squamous cell carcinoma and other lymphomas, in the scar capsule around breast implants, and has issued safety communications about them.

sections.title: Mammograms when you have implants
sections.body: If you have breast implants you should still have regular screening mammograms, unless all breast tissue was removed by a double mastectomy before the implants were placed.

items.title: Tell them when you book
items.text: Say that you have implants, so you can check that the centre is experienced in imaging people with implants.

items.title: Tell the technologist
items.text: Tell the person taking your mammogram about your implants before it starts.

items.title: Extra pictures
items.text: Usually four extra images are taken (two of each breast), with the implant gently pushed back so more breast tissue can be seen.
items.note: Implants can hide some breast tissue on a mammogram. Rupture during a mammogram is very rare.

items.title: After reconstruction
items.text: A breast rebuilt after a mastectomy usually does not need mammograms; it is checked by physical exams. The other breast still has mammograms.

Ductal carcinoma in situ: abnormal cells inside the milk ducts that have not spread into surrounding tissue (stage 0).

Invasive ductal carcinoma: cancer that starts in a duct and grows into nearby breast tissue.
Invasive lobular carcinoma: cancer that starts in a lobule and grows into nearby breast tissue.

faqs.question: Is every breast lump cancer?
faqs.answer: No. Most breast lumps are not cancer; many are cysts or fibroadenomas. Any new or changing lump should still be checked by a doctor, because only tests can tell for sure.

faqs.question: How do I check my own breasts?
faqs.answer: Touch your whole breast area up to your collarbone and armpits, look for changes in size, shape, skin or nipples, and see a doctor about anything new. There is no special technique; checking regularly is what matters. It does not replace mammograms.

faqs.question: Can men get breast cancer?
faqs.answer: Yes. It is rare, but men have breast tissue and can develop breast cancer. Men should also get a new lump or nipple change checked.

faqs.question: What is the difference between grade and stage?
faqs.answer: Grade describes how abnormal the cancer cells look under the microscope. Stage describes how big the cancer is and how far it has spread. They are measured separately.

faqs.question: What does triple-negative mean?
faqs.answer: The cancer cells do not have estrogen or progesterone receptors and do not have too much HER2. Hormone therapy and HER2 drugs do not work for it, so chemotherapy is usually the main treatment.

faqs.question: Does a BI-RADS 4 or 5 result mean I have cancer?
faqs.answer: No. BI-RADS describes how suspicious a finding looks on imaging. Only a biopsy can confirm cancer. A BI-RADS 4 or 5 result means a biopsy is recommended.

faqs.question: If I have a risk factor, will I get breast cancer?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. Many people with risk factors never get breast cancer, and many who do have no risk factor besides being a woman and getting older.

faqs.question: Can I prevent breast cancer completely?
faqs.answer: No. Staying active, keeping a healthy weight and limiting alcohol are linked to lower risk, but nothing removes the risk completely. Screening helps find cancer early.

faqs.question: Is the AI result on this website a diagnosis?
faqs.answer: No. It is an estimate for research and education only. Only a doctor, with imaging, a biopsy and pathology, can diagnose breast cancer.

faqs.question: Where can I find reliable information?
faqs.answer: Trusted sources include the World Health Organization, the National Cancer Institute, the American Cancer Society, Breast Cancer Now and RadiologyInfo.org. Each module here lists its references.

faqs.question: Do breast implants cause breast cancer?
faqs.answer: Breast implants have not been shown to increase breast cancer risk. They are linked to a rare lymphoma called BIA-ALCL, so swelling, a lump or pain around an implant should be checked. People with implants should still have screening mammograms.
